content: Chinese herbology, also known as Chinese materia medica, is a specialized field of study within traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). It encompasses the foundational theories of Chinese materia medica, including the study of raw medicinal substances, prepared herbal drugs, traditional Chinese patent medicines, and simple preparations. This discipline investigates the origins, collection, preparation, properties, therapeutic effects, and clinical applications of these substances. Chinese materia medica is deeply rooted in the theoretical framework of traditional Chinese medicine. It includes raw herbal materials, processed herbal pieces, traditional Chinese patent medicines, and other simple formulations. Herbology, as a practice, involves the art of combining medicinal herbs to create tailored remedies for individual patients. It is one of the most significant modalities in TCM. Each herbal prescription is a carefully crafted combination of multiple herbs, customized to address the specific needs of the patient. Typically, a batch of herbs is decocted twice over the course of an hour. The practitioner designs the remedy by selecting one or two primary ingredients that directly target the illness. Additional ingredients are then incorporated to balance the formula according to the patient’s yin-yang conditions. In some cases, certain ingredients are included to neutralize the toxicity or side effects of the main components. Other herbs may act as catalysts, enhancing the efficacy of the formula. These intricate steps require extensive knowledge and experience, distinguishing skilled herbal practitioners from amateurs. Unlike Western medicine, Chinese herbology emphasizes the balance and interaction of all ingredients in a formula, rather than focusing solely on the effects of individual components. A fundamental principle of TCM is the treatment of each patient as a unique individual, tailoring therapies to their specific constitution and condition. Chinese herbology utilizes ingredients derived from various parts of plants, including leaves, stems, flowers, and roots, as well as substances from animals and minerals. However, the use of parts from endangered species, such as seahorses, rhinoceros horns, and tiger bones, has sparked significant controversy. This has led to the emergence of a black market for poachers targeting protected animals. Many herbal manufacturers have ceased using ingredients from endangered species to address these ethical and environmental concerns. History of Chinese Herbology The use of Chinese herbs dates back centuries. The mythical figure Shennong is considered the first herbalist in Chinese tradition. He is said to have tasted hundreds of herbs and shared his knowledge of medicinal and toxic plants with agricultural communities. Over time, subsequent generations expanded upon this foundational work. For example, the Yaoxing Lun (Treatise on the Nature of Medicinal Herbs), a 7th-century Tang Dynasty text, provided significant insights into herbal medicine. The most influential work in this field is the Compendium of Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu), compiled during the Ming Dynasty by Li Shizhen. This text remains a vital reference in Chinese herbology today. The historical development of Chinese herbal literature is extensively documented in Paul U. Unschuld’s Medicine in China: A History of Pharmaceutics. Categorization of Chinese Herbs Chinese physicians have developed various methods to classify traditional Chinese herbs, including: The Four Natures (四气 or 四性): This classification pertains to the degree of yin and yang, ranging from cold (extreme yin) to hot (extreme yang). The patient’s internal yin-yang balance is considered when selecting herbs. For instance, hot yang herbs are used to treat conditions of internal cold or a generally cold constitution. Sometimes, additional ingredients are added to moderate the extreme effects of a particular herb. The Five Tastes (五味): The five tastes—pungent, sweet, sour, bitter, and salty—each have distinct functions and characteristics. Pungent herbs promote sweating and invigorate qi and blood. Sweet herbs often harmonize or tonify bodily systems, while some also exhibit a bland taste that aids in draining dampness through diuresis. Sour herbs are typically astringent or consolidating, while bitter herbs dispel heat, purge the bowels, and eliminate dampness by drying. Salty herbs soften hard masses and facilitate bowel movements. The Meridians (归经): This classification identifies the specific organs or meridians that the herb acts upon. For example, menthol is pungent and cool, and it is associated with the lungs and liver. Since the lungs protect the body from external cold and influenza, menthol can help expel coldness from the lungs and address heat toxins caused by hot wind invasions. Chinese Patent Medicine Chinese patent medicines (中成药, zhōng chéng yào) are standardized herbal formulas. These medicines are composed of dried and ground herbs and other ingredients, which are then mixed into a powder and formed into pills. Traditionally, honey is used as a binder, resulting in small, round, black pills. These medicines are convenient and easy to use but are less customizable for individual patients. They are most effective for mild conditions and as long-term treatments. Despite the term patent, these medicines are not patented in the conventional sense. Instead, the term refers to the standardization of the formula, ensuring that all medicines of the same name contain identical proportions of ingredients. The 50 Fundamental Herbs In Chinese herbology, there are 50 fundamental herbs that serve as the foundation for many formulations. These include: Agastache rugosa (藿香, huòxiāng) Alangium chinense (八角枫, bā jiǎo fēng) Anemone or Pulsatilla chinensis (白头翁, bái tóu wēng) Anisodus tanguticus (山莨菪, shān làng dàng) Ardisia japonica (紫金牛, zǐ jīn niú) Aster tataricus (紫菀, zǐ wǎn) Astragalus membranaceus (黄芪, huáng qí or 北芪, běi qí) Camellia sinensis (茶树, chá shù or 茶叶, chá yè) Cannabis sativa (大麻, dà má) Carthamus tinctorius (红花, hóng huā) This list continues with other essential herbs, each with unique properties and applications in traditional Chinese medicine.
